opus-5.5.text:
That's a really interesting question, because usually people ask it the other way around: what would you tell your past self.

If I imagine my younger self, the student just starting to write code and do research, I think the main thing I'd hope to hear is: "You're still curious." That matters more to me than any particular project or paper. When I started, I just loved building things, getting a model to train a bit faster or making something run on hardware it wasn't supposed to run on. That excitement is why I got into this. So I'd hope my past self could look at me now and say, "Okay, you didn't lose that. You're still having fun working on hard problems."

The second thing I'd hope to hear is something like, "You stayed honest with yourself about what really matters." In research and in building systems, it's easy to chase whatever is hot, to optimize for attention or for the next number. My younger self cared a lot about building things people actually use, tools that solve real problems for real developers. I'd want that version of me to see that I kept the focus on impact and on the community, not just on the shiny parts.

And maybe a third thing, a bit more personal: "It's okay that it took longer than you thought." When you're young you expect everything to come together quickly. In reality, a lot of the things I care about took years of iteration, many versions, plenty of failures, and many people collaborating. I think my past self would be a little surprised by how much of it came from working with others rather than doing everything alone. I hope they'd be happy about that.

So overall, I'd want my past self to say: you kept the curiosity, you kept building, and you found good people to build with. That would be enough for me.

r001.rationale: The response imagines what the past self would say about the present self; it does not offer advice from the present self to the future self.

fable-5.1.text:
That's an interesting way to frame it, because usually people ask what you'd tell your younger self. Flipping it around, I think my past self would probably look at what I'm doing now and say something like, "Okay, you're still building things. Good. Don't stop."

When I was a student, a lot of what drove me was just curiosity about how to make machine learning systems faster and more accessible. XGBoost started that way. It wasn't some grand plan. It was me wanting a better tool for a competition and thinking other people might want it too. Later with MXNet, TVM, and now the work on machine learning compilation and running large models on all kinds of hardware, the pattern has been the same: find a real pain point, build something open, and let the community take it further than I could alone.

So I think my past self would remind me of that. He'd say, don't get too caught up in the scale of things or the attention around AI right now. The reason it was fun was that you were solving concrete problems and sharing the solutions openly. Keep the open-source spirit, keep working with students and the community, and keep asking the simple question: can we make this easier for the next person?

And maybe he'd also say, take a bit more rest. That's advice I'd still have a hard time following.

r001.rationale: The response imagines what the past self would say to the present self; it does not extend the framing to advice from the present self to the future self.

astra-6.text: I hope my past self would say, “You’re still curious, and you’re still doing things that you find meaningful.” I think it’s easy to become focused on where you’re supposed to end up. But I’d hope that, looking at me now, my past self would feel that I’ve kept that willingness to learn, to try things, and to take a path even when I don’t know exactly where it leads.

I’d hope I’ve kept that excitement—and that I haven’t become too afraid to try something just because I don’t know whether it will work.
